Item batteries

Source: vignettes/articles/table-battery.Rmd
table-battery.Rmd
library(spicy)

A battery is a set of items that respondents rate on the same scale: a Likert grid, a block of satisfaction questions, the “array” question of a survey tool. table_battery() gives each item one row and each level of the scale one column. The percentages are row percentages, and the last column gives the base of each row. Items can then be compared at a glance, which a table with one block of rows per item does not allow.

The function is experimental in this release: its arguments and its output may still change.

The data

The sochealth data hold four items rated from 1 to 5: satisfaction with health, work, relationships and standard of living. They are integer columns. Giving them the labels of the scale makes the table readable:

scale_labels <- c(
  "Very dissatisfied",
  "Dissatisfied",
  "Neutral",
  "Satisfied",
  "Very satisfied"
)
sat <- sochealth[c("sex", "age_group", "weight")]
for (v in grep("^life_sat_", names(sochealth), value = TRUE)) {
  sat[[v]] <- factor(sochealth[[v]], levels = 1:5, labels = scale_labels)
  attr(sat[[v]], "label") <- attr(sochealth[[v]], "label")
}

The items share one scale. Factors, and labelled columns with value labels, must declare the same levels: an item whose levels differ is an error that names it, so a typo in one recode does not go unnoticed. Numeric and text items take the union of the values they hold, so a level that only one item holds is a column of every item. levels gives the scale outright: the integer items of sochealth can be tabulated as they are with levels = 1:5, which also keeps a level that nobody chose.

A first table 

table_battery(sat, select = starts_with("life_sat_"), labels = TRUE)
#> Item battery
#> 
#>  Variable                                   │ Very dissatisfied  Dissatisfied 
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────
#>  Satisfaction with health (1-5)             │        7.4             14.2     
#>  Satisfaction with work (1-5)               │        7.6             16.3     
#>  Satisfaction with relationships (1-5)      │        3.1             10.9     
#>  Satisfaction with standard of living (1-5) │        6.4             17.1     
#> 
#>  Variable                                   │ Neutral  Satisfied 
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────
#>  Satisfaction with health (1-5)             │  24.0      25.1    
#>  Satisfaction with work (1-5)               │  26.4      30.3    
#>  Satisfaction with relationships (1-5)      │  26.3      29.7    
#>  Satisfaction with standard of living (1-5) │  26.0      31.5    
#> 
#>  Variable                                   │ Very satisfied   n   
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────
#>  Satisfaction with health (1-5)             │      29.4       1192 
#>  Satisfaction with work (1-5)               │      19.5       1192 
#>  Satisfaction with relationships (1-5)      │      29.9       1192 
#>  Satisfaction with standard of living (1-5) │      19.0       1192 
#> 
#> Note. Percentages are row percentages. Base: respondents who answered the item.

Each row sums to 100. The base n is the number of respondents who answered the item, so it can differ from one item to the next. A level that nobody chose keeps its column, at 0: it was offered and not chosen, which is worth reporting.

Levels and base

levels chooses the levels shown and their order. A level left out leaves the percentages and the base, and the note names it. This is the way to keep a “Don’t know” answer out of the base. Here the neutral level is left out:

table_battery(
  sat,
  select = starts_with("life_sat_"),
  levels = scale_labels[-3]
)
#> Item battery
#> 
#>  Variable               │ Very dissatisfied  Dissatisfied  Satisfied 
#> ────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  life_sat_health        │        9.7             18.7        33.0    
#>  life_sat_work          │       10.3             22.1        41.2    
#>  life_sat_relationships │        4.2             14.8        40.3    
#>  life_sat_standard      │        8.6             23.1        42.5    
#> 
#>  Variable               │ Very satisfied   n  
#> ────────────────────────┼─────────────────────
#>  life_sat_health        │      38.6       906 
#>  life_sat_work          │      26.5       877 
#>  life_sat_relationships │      40.7       878 
#>  life_sat_standard      │      25.7       882 
#> 
#> Note. Percentages are row percentages. Base: respondents who answered the item. Answers left out of the percentages and the base: Neutral.

By default the missing answers leave the base. With drop_na = FALSE, a column of missing answers follows the levels and the base of each item becomes every respondent:

table_battery(
  sat,
  select = starts_with("life_sat_"),
  drop_na = FALSE
)
#> Item battery
#> 
#>  Variable               │ Very dissatisfied  Dissatisfied  Neutral  Satisfied 
#> ────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  life_sat_health        │        7.3             14.1       23.8      24.9    
#>  life_sat_work          │        7.5             16.2       26.2      30.1    
#>  life_sat_relationships │        3.1             10.8       26.2      29.5    
#>  life_sat_standard      │        6.3             17.0       25.8      31.2    
#> 
#>  Variable               │ Very satisfied  (Missing)   n   
#> ────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────
#>  life_sat_health        │      29.2          0.7     1200 
#>  life_sat_work          │      19.3          0.7     1200 
#>  life_sat_relationships │      29.8          0.7     1200 
#>  life_sat_standard      │      18.9          0.7     1200 
#> 
#> Note. Percentages are row percentages. Base: all respondents, including those who did not answer the item.

The top of the scale and the order of the rows

top adds a summary column, the sum of the percentages of some levels. Its header lists them, joined by +. sort orders the rows, with the suffix grammar of freq(): + for increasing and - for decreasing order, after top (the summary column), name (the labels) or a level ("Neutral-"). "-" alone sorts on the summary column. Whole percentages are enough to compare the items, and percent_digits = 0 prints them:

table_battery(
  sat,
  select = starts_with("life_sat_"),
  labels = TRUE,
  top = c("Very satisfied", "Satisfied"),
  sort = "top-",
  percent_digits = 0
)
#> Item battery
#> 
#>  Variable                                   │ Very dissatisfied  Dissatisfied 
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────
#>  Satisfaction with relationships (1-5)      │         3               11      
#>  Satisfaction with health (1-5)             │         7               14      
#>  Satisfaction with standard of living (1-5) │         6               17      
#>  Satisfaction with work (1-5)               │         8               16      
#> 
#>  Variable                                   │ Neutral  Satisfied 
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────
#>  Satisfaction with relationships (1-5)      │   26        30     
#>  Satisfaction with health (1-5)             │   24        25     
#>  Satisfaction with standard of living (1-5) │   26        31     
#>  Satisfaction with work (1-5)               │   26        30     
#> 
#>  Variable                                   │ Very satisfied 
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────────────
#>  Satisfaction with relationships (1-5)      │       30       
#>  Satisfaction with health (1-5)             │       29       
#>  Satisfaction with standard of living (1-5) │       19       
#>  Satisfaction with work (1-5)               │       19       
#> 
#>  Variable                                   │ Very satisfied + Satisfied   n   
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────
#>  Satisfaction with relationships (1-5)      │             60              1192 
#>  Satisfaction with health (1-5)             │             54              1192 
#>  Satisfaction with standard of living (1-5) │             51              1192 
#>  Satisfaction with work (1-5)               │             50              1192 
#> 
#> Note. Percentages are row percentages. Base: respondents who answered the item.

Comparing groups

With by, each group gets a block of columns, and each item a test of independence of the item and the group. The test is the chi-squared test, or Fisher’s exact test when an expected count is below 5, as in table_categorical(). The items of a battery are read together, so the p-values are adjusted for the family of the items by Holm’s method, as in table_multiresponse():

table_battery(sat, select = starts_with("life_sat_"), by = sex)
#> Item battery by sex
#> 
#>  Variable               │ Female Very dissatisfied  Female Dissatisfied 
#> ────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  life_sat_health        │           7.6                    14.4         
#>  life_sat_work          │           8.1                    16.9         
#>  life_sat_relationships │           3.6                    10.2         
#>  life_sat_standard      │           6.2                    18.9         
#> 
#>  Variable               │ Female Neutral  Female Satisfied 
#> ────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────
#>  life_sat_health        │      25.0             25.2       
#>  life_sat_work          │      25.9             33.2       
#>  life_sat_relationships │      26.3             31.5       
#>  life_sat_standard      │      24.1             33.3       
#> 
#>  Variable               │ Female Very satisfied  Female n 
#> ────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────
#>  life_sat_health        │         27.8             616    
#>  life_sat_work          │         15.9             615    
#>  life_sat_relationships │         28.3             615    
#>  life_sat_standard      │         17.6             615    
#> 
#>  Variable               │ Male Very dissatisfied  Male Dissatisfied

#>  life_sat_work          │          6.9                  15.6        
#>  life_sat_relationships │          2.6                  11.6        
#>  life_sat_standard      │          6.6                  15.3        
#> 
#>  Variable               │ Male Neutral  Male Satisfied  Male Very satisfied 
#> ────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  life_sat_health        │     22.9           25.0              31.1         
#>  life_sat_work          │     27.0           27.2              23.2         
#>  life_sat_relationships │     26.3           27.7              31.7         
#>  life_sat_standard      │     28.1           29.5              20.6         
#> 
#>  Variable               │ Male n   p   
#> ────────────────────────┼──────────────

A wide table is printed in panels that fit the console, the item labels repeated in each. With top, each group keeps only the summary column and its base, the usual table for comparing groups:

table_battery(
  sat,
  select = starts_with("life_sat_"),
  by = age_group,
  labels = TRUE,
  top = c("Very satisfied", "Satisfied")
)
#> Item battery by Age group

p_adjust = "none" reports the raw p-values, and p_value = FALSE removes the tests. test chooses another test, as in table_categorical().

Weights

weights takes frequency weights, as in table_categorical(). The counts, the percentages, the base and the tests are weighted, and the note says so:

table_battery(
  sat,
  select = starts_with("life_sat_"),
  weights = weight,
  top = c("Very satisfied", "Satisfied")
)
#> Item battery
#> 
#>  Variable               │ Very dissatisfied  Dissatisfied  Neutral  Satisfied 
#> ────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  life_sat_health        │        7.4             14.3       24.6      25.0    
#>  life_sat_work          │        7.8             16.1       26.5      29.7    
#>  life_sat_relationships │        3.1             10.3       26.9      29.4    
#>  life_sat_standard      │        6.2             17.3       26.1      31.4    
#> 
#>  Variable               │ Very satisfied  Very satisfied + Satisfied   n   
#> ────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  life_sat_health        │      28.6                  53.7             1191 
#>  life_sat_work          │      20.0                  49.7             1189 
#>  life_sat_relationships │      30.2                  59.7             1188 
#>  life_sat_standard      │      19.1                  50.4             1188 
#> 
#> Note. Percentages are row percentages. Base: respondents who answered the item. Statistics weighted by weight.

The percentages of a survey are right under its weights, but its tests need the design. A design-based version of this table is planned.

Data frames

output = "data.frame" returns the displayed table with its numbers, one row per item:

table_battery(
  sat,
  select = starts_with("life_sat_"),
  by = sex,
  top = c("Very satisfied", "Satisfied"),
  output = "data.frame"
)
#>                 variable                  label
#> 1        life_sat_health        life_sat_health
#> 2          life_sat_work          life_sat_work
#> 3 life_sat_relationships life_sat_relationships
#> 4      life_sat_standard      life_sat_standard
#>   Female Very satisfied + Satisfied Female n Male Very satisfied + Satisfied
#> 1                          52.92208      616                        56.07639
#> 2                          49.10569      615                        50.43328
#> 3                          59.83740      615                        59.44541
#> 4                          50.89431      615                        50.08666
#>   Male n          p
#> 1    576 0.79829346
#> 2    577 0.05232225
#> 3    577 0.79829346
#> 4    577 0.39656912

output = "long" returns one row per item, group and level, with the test of each item:

long <- table_battery(
  sat,
  select = starts_with("life_sat_"),
  by = sex,
  output = "long"
)
head(long)
#>          variable           label  group             level .row_role   n
#> 1 life_sat_health life_sat_health Female Very dissatisfied     level  47
#> 2 life_sat_health life_sat_health Female      Dissatisfied     level  89
#> 3 life_sat_health life_sat_health Female           Neutral     level 154
#> 4 life_sat_health life_sat_health Female         Satisfied     level 155
#> 5 life_sat_health life_sat_health Female    Very satisfied     level 171
#> 6 life_sat_health life_sat_health   Male Very dissatisfied     level  41
#>         pct   test_type statistic df   p.value p_unadjusted
#> 1  7.629870 chi_squared  1.828005  4 0.7982935     0.767355
#> 2 14.448052 chi_squared  1.828005  4 0.7982935     0.767355
#> 3 25.000000 chi_squared  1.828005  4 0.7982935     0.767355
#> 4 25.162338 chi_squared  1.828005  4 0.7982935     0.767355
#> 5 27.759740 chi_squared  1.828005  4 0.7982935     0.767355
#> 6  7.118056 chi_squared  1.828005  4 0.7982935     0.767355

inline() cites a cell in running text: the item, then the level of the scale, and the group with model:

tbl <- table_battery(sat, select = starts_with("life_sat_"), by = sex)
inline(tbl, life_sat_work, "Very satisfied", "pct", model = "Female")
#> [1] "15.9"

Output engines

The same table renders through six further engines, the console being the reference.

table_battery(sat, select = starts_with("life_sat_"), output = "gt")
table_battery(sat, select = starts_with("life_sat_"), output = "tinytable")
table_battery(sat, select = starts_with("life_sat_"), output = "flextable")
table_battery(
  sat,
  select = starts_with("life_sat_"),
  output = "excel",
  excel_path = "satisfaction.xlsx"
)
table_battery(
  sat,
  select = starts_with("life_sat_"),
  output = "word",
  word_path = "satisfaction.docx"
)
table_battery(sat, select = starts_with("life_sat_"), output = "clipboard")

Rendered output 

pkgdown_dark_gt(
  table_battery(
    sat,
    select = starts_with("life_sat_"),
    by = sex,
    labels = TRUE,
    top = c("Very satisfied", "Satisfied"),
    output = "gt"
  )
)
